test_text.title: Saving bugs to find new drugs

article.title: Saving bugs to find new drugs

items.sentence_raw: More drugs than you might think are derived from, or inspired by, compounds found in living things.
Looking to nature for the soothing and curing of our ailments is nothing new - we have been doing it for tens of thousands of years.

You only have to look at other primates - such as the capuchin monkeys who rub themselves with toxin-oozing millipedes to deter mosquitoes, or the chimpanzees who use noxious forest plants to rid themselves of intestinal parasites - to realise that our ancient ancestors too probably had a basic grasp of medicine.
items.explain: Q16: The question asks for **examples of animals** using **medicinal substances from nature**. The passage mentions *'capuchin monkeys who rub themselves with toxin-oozing millipedes'* and *'chimpanzees who use noxious forest plants'* — these are animals using natural things as medicine. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: Pharmaceutical science and chemistry built on these ancient foundations and perfected the extraction, characterisation, modification and testing of these natural products.
Then, for a while, modern pharmaceutical science moved its focus away from nature and into the laboratory, designing chemical compounds from scratch.
The main cause of this shift is that although there are plenty of promising chemical compounds in nature, finding them is far from easy.
items.explain: Q19: The question asks for a **reason** why **nature-based medicines fell out of favour**. The passage says *'The main cause of this shift is that... finding them is far from easy'* — **'this shift'** refers to moving away from nature, and the difficulty of finding compounds is the **reason**. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Securing sufficient numbers of the organism in question, isolating and characterising the compounds of interest, and producing large quantities of these compounds are all significant hurdles.
Laboratory-based drug discovery has achieved varying levels of success, something which has now prompted the development of new approaches focusing once again on natural products.
With the ability to mine genomes for useful compounds, it is now evident that we have barely scratched the surface of nature's molecular diversity.
This realisation, together with several looming health crises, such as antibiotic resistance, has put bioprospecting - the search for useful compounds in nature - firmly back on the map.
items.explain: Q14: The question asks about **factors** that caused a **renewed interest** in natural medicines. The passage says *'several looming health crises, such as antibiotic resistance, has put bioprospecting... firmly back on the map'* — **'looming health crises'** are the **factors**, and **'back on the map'** means **renewed interest**. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: Insects are the undisputed masters of the terrestrial domain, where they occupy every possible niche.

Consequently, they have a bewildering array of interactions with other organisms, something which has driven the evolution of an enormous range of very interesting compounds for defensive and offensive purposes.
items.explain:
Q21: The question asks what makes insects **interesting** for drug research. The passage says insects have *'an enormous range of very interesting compounds for defensive and offensive purposes'* — **'defensive'** compounds are substances to **protect themselves**. This matches option **B**. ***Option A is a trap*** — the passage talks about the **variety of species**, not the **huge number of individual insects**. So the answer is **B**.

Q22: The question asks what makes insects **interesting** for drug research. The passage says insects have *'an enormous range of very interesting compounds for defensive and offensive purposes'* — **'defensive'** compounds are substances to **protect themselves**. This matches option **B**. ***Option A is a trap*** — the passage talks about the **variety of species**, not the **huge number of individual insects**. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Their remarkable diversity exceeds that of every other group of animals on the planet combined.
Yet even though insects are far and away the most diverse animals in existence, their potential as sources of therapeutic compounds is yet to be realised.
From the tiny proportion of insects that have been investigated, several promising compounds have been identified.
For example, alloferon, an antimicrobial compound produced by blow fly larvae, is used as an antiviral and antitumor agent in South Korea and Russia.
items.explain: Q20: The question asks for an **example of an insect-derived medicine in use** right now. The passage says *'alloferon, an antimicrobial compound produced by blow fly larvae, is used as an antiviral and antitumor agent in South Korea and Russia'* — this is a medicine from insects being used **at the moment**. So the answer is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: The larvae of a few other insect species are being investigated for the potent antimicrobial compounds they produce.
Meanwhile, a compound from the venom of the wasp Polybia paulista has potential in cancer treatment.
Why is it that insects have received relatively little attention in bioprospecting?
Firstly, there are so many insects that, without some manner of targeted approach, investigating this huge variety of species is a daunting task.
items.explain: Q17: The question asks for **reasons** why using insects in drug research is **challenging**. The passage lists problems: insects are *'very small'*, their glands are *'smaller still'*, making it *'difficult to obtain sufficient quantities'*, and many species are *'difficult to rear in captivity'*. All these are **reasons** for the challenge. So the answer is **F**.

items.sentence_raw: Secondly, insects are generally very small, and the glands inside them that secrete potentially useful compounds are smaller still.
This can make it difficult to obtain sufficient quantities of the compound for subsequent testing.
items.explain: Q17: The question asks for **reasons** why using insects in drug research is **challenging**. The passage lists problems: insects are *'very small'*, their glands are *'smaller still'*, making it *'difficult to obtain sufficient quantities'*, and many species are *'difficult to rear in captivity'*. All these are **reasons** for the challenge. So the answer is **F**.

items.sentence_raw: Thirdly, although we consider insects to be everywhere, the reality of this ubiquity is vast numbers of a few extremely common species.
Many insect species are infrequently encountered and very difficult to rear in captivity, which, again, can leave us with insufficient material to work with.
items.explain: Q17: The question asks for **reasons** why using insects in drug research is **challenging**. The passage lists problems: insects are *'very small'*, their glands are *'smaller still'*, making it *'difficult to obtain sufficient quantities'*, and many species are *'difficult to rear in captivity'*. All these are **reasons** for the challenge. So the answer is **F**.

items.sentence_raw: My colleagues and I at Aberystwyth University in the UK have developed an approach in which we use our knowledge of ecology as a guide to target our efforts.
items.explain: Q23: The passage says *'we use our knowledge of ecology as a guide to target our efforts'* — their **expertise** is in **ecology**. So the answer is **ecology**.

items.sentence_raw: The creatures that particularly interest us are the many insects that secrete powerful poison for subduing prey and keeping it fresh for future consumption.
items.explain: Q24: The passage says insects secrete poison for *'subduing prey and keeping it fresh for future consumption'* — **'subduing'** means to overpower, and **'keeping it fresh'** means to preserve their **prey**. So the answer is **prey**.

items.sentence_raw: There are even more insects that are masters of exploiting filthy habitats, such as faeces and carcasses, where they are regularly challenged by thousands of micro-organisms.
items.explain: Q25: The passage says insects are *'masters of exploiting filthy habitats, such as faeces and carcasses'* — these are the **habitats** where they face micro-organisms. So the answer is **habitats**.

items.sentence_raw: These insects have many antimicrobial compounds for dealing with pathogenic bacteria and fungi, suggesting that there is certainly potential to find many compounds that can serve as or inspire new antibiotics.
items.explain: Q26: The passage says these compounds can *'serve as or inspire new antibiotics'* — the drugs Piper hopes to develop are **antibiotics**. So the answer is **antibiotics**.

items.sentence_raw: Although natural history knowledge points us in the right direction, it doesn't solve the problems associated with obtaining useful compounds from insects.

Fortunately, it is now possible to snip out the stretches of the insect's DNA that carry the codes for the interesting compounds and insert them into cell lines that allow larger quantities to be produced.
items.explain: Q15: The question asks about **recent technological advances** that made insect research **easier**. The passage says *'it is now possible to snip out the stretches of the insect's DNA... and insert them into cell lines that allow larger quantities to be produced'* — this DNA technology is a **recent advance** that solves the problem of getting enough material. So the answer is **H**.

items.sentence_raw: And although the road from isolating and characterising compounds with desirable qualities to developing a commercial product is very long and full of pitfalls, the variety of successful animal-derived pharmaceuticals on the market demonstrates there is a precedent here that is worth exploring.
With every bit of wilderness that disappears, we deprive ourselves of potential medicines.
As much as I'd love to help develop a groundbreaking insect-derived medicine, my main motivation for looking at insects in this way is conservation.
I sincerely believe that all species, however small and seemingly insignificant, have a right to exist for their own sake.

If we can shine a light on the darker recesses of nature's medicine cabinet, exploring the useful chemistry of the most diverse animals on the planet, I believe we can make people think differently about the value of nature.
items.explain: Q18: The question asks how **interest in drug research** may **benefit wildlife**. The passage says exploring nature's chemistry can *'make people think differently about the value of nature'* — this changed thinking is a **benefit** for **wildlife** conservation. So the answer is **I**.

subtitles: Zoologist Ross Piper looks at the potential of insects in pharmaceutical research
